## Results

We screened public human RNA-seq libraries for papillomavirus reads under three discovery strategies (Methods): an unbiased prevalence sweep of skin and related tissues (`r comma(stats$n_screened)` libraries screened), a targeted query of productive cutaneous lesions providing positive controls (`r stats$n_targeted` wart/epidermodysplasia-verruciformis skin libraries), and a broadened skin-neoplasia sweep capturing cSCC, actinic keratosis (AK) and Bowen disease (`r comma(stats$n_csc)` libraries screened). Throughout, every screened library, including HPV-negative ones, was scored as papillomavirus reads per million so that infection burden could be separated from sequencing depth, and each sample was annotated as primary tissue, cell line, or engineered material.

### HPV signal in public RNA-seq is dominated by cell-line and engineered artifacts

In the unbiased sweep, HPV positivity was strongly concentrated in non-primary material. Engineered libraries were HPV-positive in `r f2(stats$eng_pct)`% of cases (95% CI `r pci(stats$eng_lo, stats$eng_hi)`) and cell-line libraries in `r f2(stats$cl_pct)`% (`r pci(stats$cl_lo, stats$cl_hi)`), versus only `r f2(stats$clin_pct)`% (`r pci(stats$clin_lo, stats$clin_hi)`) of clinical primary-tissue libraries (@tbl-positivity). In logistic regression this corresponded to roughly five-fold higher odds of positivity for engineered (OR `r fo(stats$eng_or)`, 95% CI `r oci(stats$eng_or_lo, stats$eng_or_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$eng_or_p)`) and cell-line (OR `r fo(stats$cl_or)`, `r oci(stats$cl_or_lo, stats$cl_or_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$cl_or_p)`) samples relative to clinical tissue (likelihood-ratio *P* = `r fp(stats$lr_p)`). These positives were almost entirely the high-risk mucosal alpha types. Of the `r stats$hpv18_tot` libraries anywhere in the cohort in which HPV18 met the assignment criterion, `r stats$hpv18_cl` were cell lines and the remaining `r stats$hpv18_tot - stats$hpv18_cl` engineered material, so no tissue library carried an assigned HPV18 at all; for HPV16, `r stats$hpv16_cl` of `r stats$hpv16_tot` were cell lines, leaving `r stats$hpv16_tot - stats$hpv16_cl` in tissue (@supptbl-types). This is the expected signature of integrated-HPV cell lines such as HeLa and of their well-documented cross-contamination of archived sequencing data. Genuine primary skin therefore carries HPV at a low rate (2–4%, below), and the apparent abundance of HPV in public transcriptomes is largely a laboratory artifact that must be partitioned out before any prevalence claim.

The transcripts themselves carry an independent signature of that artifact, in two forms. E1 and E2 are encoded on the same early polycistronic message, so their read counts should track one another; integration characteristically disrupts the E2 open reading frame while sparing E1, inverting the ratio. Cell-line libraries show a median E1:E2 ratio of `r fo(stats$e1e2_cl)`, against `r formatC(stats$e1e2_ctrl, format="f", digits=2)` in productive controls, `r formatC(stats$e1e2_skin, format="f", digits=2)` in unselected skin and `r formatC(stats$e1e2_neo, format="f", digits=2)` in neoplasia, and the ratio separates cell lines from productive primary infection almost completely (AUC 0.97, Wilcoxon *P* = 2.8×10⁻¹⁴; @fig-integration a). Where integration has gone further and the early region is lost but for E6 and E7, both E1 and E2 fall silent and no ratio can be formed; those libraries instead show oncogene transcription with no late transcription at all, the canonical integrated-carcinoma pattern, and are captured by that criterion. Together the two signatures call `r pp(stats$e1e2_cl_pct)`% of `r stats$e1e2_cl_n` cell-line libraries as integration-like (`r stats$e1e2_cl_ratio` by the inverted ratio, `r stats$e1e2_cl_e67` by the E6/E7-only pattern the ratio cannot see) while calling `r pp(stats$e1e2_ev_pct)`% of EV biopsies and `r pp(stats$e1e2_ctrl_pct)`% of productive controls, the two groups where infection is episomal by definition. That it reports integration rather than culture is settled by the one cell line in the cohort that maintains its genome episomally, an HPV31-positive HaCaT derivative, which sits at 0.6–1.0 alongside primary tissue rather than with the integrated lines. Applied as a detector, the ratio flags `r stats$e1e2_disc` libraries that carry the integration signature without being labeled as cell lines, including melanoma lines under shRNA knockdown recorded with a tissue source of "skin" and cutaneous SCC lines recorded with a carcinoma diagnosis, which is what motivates the engineered group above. The ratio was checked against the event it claims to report. Calling virus–host chimeric reads against a combined human/HPV index in `r stats$jx_n` libraries spanning the range of the ratio separates the same groups completely (@fig-integration b), provided integration is scored as a *recurrent* junction rather than a raw count: the fraction of a library's junctions falling at its single most-supported site is `r stats$jx_int_range` where the ratio indicates integration and `r stats$jx_epi_range` where it does not, with no overlap. Raw counts are misleading in the opposite direction, since the two epidermodysplasia-verruciformis libraries generate the largest number of junctions in the panel while being episomal. The positive controls recover the expected answer unprompted: `r stats$jx_cl_int` of `r stats$jx_cl_n` cell-line libraries are integration-positive, and two independently return the same junction at chromosome 8q24, the documented integration site of the HeLa lineage.

The ratio was then read against a progression in which the answer is known independently. A cervical series (SRP252916) sequenced HPV16-positive normal epithelium, high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) and squamous carcinoma, six cases per arm under one rRNA-depleted protocol, alongside six HPV-negative normal controls; the arms are the submitting study's, and the tissue and the progression are ones the marker was not developed on. The HPV-negative controls returned no HPV of any type, and across the three positive arms the median ratio rises monotonically with grade. In @fig-integration c, plotted on the log~2~ scale, it runs from `r formatC(2^stats$cxg_norm, format="f", digits=2)` in normal epithelium (*n* = `r stats$cxg_norm_n`) through `r formatC(2^stats$cxg_hsil, format="f", digits=2)` in HSIL (*n* = `r stats$cxg_hsil_n`) to `r formatC(2^stats$cxg_scc, format="f", digits=2)` in carcinoma (*n* = `r stats$cxg_scc_n`), a `r formatC(2^(stats$cxg_scc - stats$cxg_norm), format="f", digits=1)`-fold rise from normal epithelium to carcinoma, in the direction integration predicts. Late transcription tracks the same axis without being part of the criterion: the libraries called episomal carry abundant L1, while those with a disrupted ratio carry almost none. The binary call is the weaker readout at this size, separating the carcinoma and lesion arms from normal epithelium (`r stats$cxg_scc_int` and `r stats$cxg_hsil_int` of six against `r stats$cxg_norm_int` of `r stats$cxg_norm_n`) but not from each other, and the normal-epithelium arm is thin: two of its six libraries yielded no HPV reads and a third carried two. The gradient, not the threshold, is what this series supports.

Cell-line and engineered libraries carry roughly five-fold higher odds of HPV positivity than primary tissue, and their positive calls are predominantly the integrated mucosal types HPV16 and HPV18, the expected signature of cell-line contamination. {#tbl-positivity}

### Skin neoplasia carries only trace HPV, not productive infection, and this is not a depth artifact

The central question, whether HPV is transcriptionally active in cSCC/AK or present only as a residual footprint, was resolved by the depth-normalized burden analysis (@fig-rpm). Productive controls (warts/condyloma) were detected at or above the control-calibrated detection floor (`r p1(stats$floor_rpm)` RPM) in `r pp(stats$ctrl_pctfloor)`% of libraries, with a median burden of `r comma(stats$ctrl_medrpm)` RPM; the EV biopsy group, sequenced most deeply of all (median `r mreads(stats$ev_medreads)` reads), reached it in `r pp(stats$ev_pctfloor)`% (median `r p1(stats$ev_medrpm)` RPM). In stark contrast, the neoplasia group reached this floor in only `r pp(stats$neo_pctfloor)`% of libraries (median `r formatC(stats$neo_medrpm, format="f", digits=3)` RPM), six orders of magnitude below the productive controls, despite being sequenced almost four times more deeply than they were (median `r mreads(stats$neo_medreads)` vs `r mreads(stats$ctrl_medreads)` reads). Unselected skin, once the EV material that the targeted queries had swept into it was reassigned to its own group (Methods), forms an almost clean null: `r pp(stats$uns_pctfloor)`% of `r comma(stats$uns_n)` libraries reach the floor.

![Depth-normalized HPV transcript burden distinguishes productive warts and EV from a trace-level signal in skin neoplasia and unselected skin. Each point is one Kraken2-screened RNA-seq library, scored as papillomavirus reads per million (RPM: Papillomaviridae clade reads ÷ (unclassified + root reads) × 10⁶) and assigned to a sample group: unselected skin (*n* = `r comma(stats$uns_n)`), cell lines (`r comma(stats$cl2_n)`), engineered cells (shRNA/siRNA knockdowns and transgenes, in-vitro material regardless of its disease label; `r comma(stats$engt_n)`), productive controls (warts/condyloma; `r stats$ctrl_n`), epidermodysplasia verruciformis biopsies (EV; `r stats$ev_n`), cutaneous neoplasia (cSCC/actinic keratosis; `r stats$neo_n`), non-permissive tissue (cutaneous adipose, which has no stratified squamous compartment in which a papillomavirus could replicate; `r stats$npt_n`), and libraries with no recorded site (`r comma(stats$oth_n)`; the residual group, 99% of which carries no site keyword in its SRA metadata rather than an identified non-cutaneous site). Points are jittered horizontally; boxes show the median and interquartile range; the *y*-axis is log~10~-scaled (RPM + 0.05). The dashed red line marks the control-calibrated detection floor (`r p1(stats$floor_rpm)` RPM, the 5th percentile of productive-control libraries). Productive controls lie far above the floor (median `r comma(stats$ctrl_medrpm)` RPM; `r pp(stats$ctrl_pctfloor)`% of libraries above floor), as do EV biopsies (`r pp(stats$ev_pctfloor)`%), whereas neoplasia and unselected skin sit near zero (`r pp(stats$neo_pctfloor)`% and `r pp(stats$uns_pctfloor)`% above floor) despite neoplasia being sequenced far more deeply than the productive controls (median `r mreads(stats$neo_medreads)` vs `r mreads(stats$ctrl_medreads)` reads). Group assignment is by metadata precedence with curated corrections (Methods): EV *cultures* (immortalized keratinocyte EV models) remain in the cell-line group, whereas the EV group holds the `r stats$ev_n` EV patient skin biopsies.](figure2.png){#fig-rpm}

This gap is not explained by sequencing depth. Modeling productive-level detection (RPM ≥ floor) as a function of sample group and log sequencing depth, productive controls exceeded unselected skin by close to four orders of magnitude (Fisher exact OR `r fo(stats$fish_or)`, 95% CI `r fo(stats$fish_lo)` to `r fo(stats$fish_hi)` under separation, *P* = `r fp(stats$fish_p)`), while neoplasia sat an order of magnitude above skin (OR `r fo(stats$m2b_or)`, 95% CI `r oci(stats$m2b_lo, stats$m2b_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2b_p)`). That contrast is easier to read on the absolute scale from which the odds ratios derive: `r stats$ctrl_pos_floor`/`r stats$ctrl_n` productive controls cross the floor, against `r stats$neo_pos_floor`/`r comma(stats$neo_n)` neoplasia libraries and `r stats$uns_pos_floor`/`r comma(stats$uns_n)` skin libraries. Neoplasia is thus measurably, but marginally, above a near-zero baseline, and remains roughly `r round(stats$ctrl_pctfloor/stats$neo_pctfloor)`-fold below the productive controls in detection rate.

Crucially, that marginal excess is not productive burden, and it is not bought by depth. Sequencing depth raised the odds of detecting *any* HPV read (OR per log₁₀ reads `r fo(stats$m2a_l10_or)`, `r oci(stats$m2a_l10_lo, stats$m2a_l10_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2a_l10_p)`), but it did not raise the odds of reaching the detection floor, either as a covariate across groups (OR `r fo(stats$m2b_l10_or)`, `r oci(stats$m2b_l10_lo, stats$m2b_l10_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2b_l10_p)`) or within the neoplasia group alone (OR `r fo(stats$neo_depth_or)`, 95% CI `r oci(stats$neo_depth_lo, stats$neo_depth_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$neo_depth_p)`). The deepest cSCC/AK libraries, at `r p1(stats$neo_maxreads)`M reads, did not cross the productive floor. Consistent with a residual footprint rather than active infection, neoplasia showed a clear excess of *trace* HPV (any read; OR `r fo(stats$m2a_or)`, 95% CI `r oci(stats$m2a_lo, stats$m2a_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2a_p)` vs unselected skin) alongside its small floor-level excess, but neither amounted to productive burden. The depth-matched detection profile confirms the same pattern non-parametrically: across every sequencing-depth bin, productive controls detect at 90–100% while neoplasia and unselected skin stay near zero (@suppfig-depth). At population scale, then, HPV in cutaneous neoplasia is a low-level, transcriptionally inactive trace, a signature consistent with the hit-and-run model, and not the productive infection seen in warts. That trace is also not integrated virus, which the junction analysis measures rather than infers: of `r stats$jx_neo_n` HPV-positive cSCC/AK libraries carrying enough viral reads to test, `r stats$jx_neo_epi` show no integration junction at all, and the `r stats$jx_neo_int` that do are HPV16 libraries the broadened query swept in from mucosal disease (@supptbl-cin), where integration is the expected state. The negatives are not limited by viral depth: integration was called in a library carrying only `r comma(stats$jx_pos_minreads)` HPV reads, and every junction-negative cSCC library exceeds that by at least `r formatC(stats$jx_neg_minfold, format="f", digits=1)`-fold.

That trace can be taken apart further, because the pipeline writes per-gene read counts for every HPV-positive library. Among the `r tr("trace_n")` below-floor libraries of unselected skin and neoplasia, `r tr("trace_pct_nogene")`% carry no reads on any HPV gene at all, a Kraken2 k-mer call that does not survive alignment and gene assignment; `r tr("trace_pct_mid")`% carry gene-mapped reads that never reach the productive threshold, `r tr("trace_mid_early")` of those `r tr("trace_mid")` being early-gene reads with the late program absent; and `r tr("trace_pct_prod")`% clear it as low-burden productive infections (@suppfig-trace). The productive controls are the mirror image, `r tr("ctrl_pct_prod")`% productive with a median late-read fraction of `r trn("ctrl_medlate")` against `r trn("trace_medlate")` across the trace. The sub-threshold signal is therefore neither wholly artifactual nor productive: a dominant technical floor overlying a minority carrying the early-without-late shape of latent or abortive infection, on the cutaneous beta and gamma types of @supptbl-trace rather than the mucosal HPV16/HPV18 that cell-line contamination would deposit.

Nor is it explained by how the libraries were built. Depth is one bound on viral-transcript recovery; RNA-selection chemistry is the other, and poly-A capture is the chemistry least favorable to it. Chemistry was resolved for `r comma(stats$chem_n)` libraries (`r pp(stats$chem_pct)`%) from SRA metadata and library-construction protocol text, and it is not balanced across groups, but the imbalance runs against the negative result rather than producing it: the neoplasia group is rRNA-depleted in `r pp(stats$chem_neo_ribo)`% of libraries against `r pp(stats$chem_skin_ribo)`% of unselected skin (@supptbl-chem), while the productive controls, the group in which productive infection is abundant, contain no rRNA-depleted libraries at all. The group in which no productive infection is found was thus built, three times more often than its comparator, with the chemistry most favorable to finding it. Within the two groups of the contrast, and adjusting for depth and group, rRNA-depleted libraries were no more likely than poly-A libraries to carry any HPV read (OR `r fo(stats$chem_ribo_or)`, 95% CI `r oci(stats$chem_ribo_lo, stats$chem_ribo_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$chem_ribo_p)`; OR `r fo(stats$chem_ribo_or_all)`, `r oci(stats$chem_ribo_lo_all, stats$chem_ribo_hi_all)` across all groups). What did move trace detection, by three- to four-fold at equal depth, was not selection chemistry but amplification: SMART template-switching (OR `r fo(stats$chem_smart_or)`) and 3'-barcoded droplet libraries (OR `r fo(stats$chem_tenx_or)`), a pattern that reads as amplification and barcode-swapping artifact rather than recovery. Adding chemistry to the models leaves both contrasts intact (trace OR `r fo(stats$m2a_or_chem)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2a_p_chem)`; floor-level OR `r fo(stats$m2b_or_chem)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2b_p_chem)`). The decisive test is to discard the ambiguity and use only the favorable chemistry: among the `r comma(stats$ribo_n)` rRNA-depleted libraries in the contrast (`r comma(stats$ribo_skin_n)` skin, `r stats$ribo_neo_n` neoplasia from `r stats$ribo_neo_studies` studies, median `r mreads(stats$ribo_neo_medreads)` and deepest `r mreads(stats$ribo_neo_maxreads)` reads), the trace excess in neoplasia is larger still (OR `r fo(stats$ribo_or)`, `r oci(stats$ribo_lo, stats$ribo_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$ribo_p)`) and not one library, in either group, reached the productive floor.

Pooling actinic keratosis with carcinoma is a choice the data support rather than an assumption. Split on diagnosis, the group comprises `r stats$ak_n` AK libraries from `r stats$ak_studies` studies and `r stats$sc_n` cSCC libraries from `r stats$sc_studies` studies (a further `r stats$mixed_n` naming both are held out as ambiguous). Both arms sit well above unselected skin, and by almost identical margins: trace HPV at OR `r fo(stats$ak_or)` for AK (*P* = `r fp(stats$ak_p)`) and OR `r fo(stats$sc_or)` for cSCC (*P* = `r fp(stats$sc_p)`), and productive-floor detection at OR `r fo(stats$ak_fl_or)` and `r fo(stats$sc_fl_or)`. Against each other they are indistinguishable on either measure, depth-adjusted: trace OR `r fo(stats$akvs_or)` (95% CI `r oci(stats$akvs_lo, stats$akvs_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$akvs_p)`), and floor-level detection `r stats$ak_floor`/`r stats$ak_n` against `r stats$sc_floor`/`r stats$sc_n` (Fisher *P* = `r fp(stats$akvf_p)`). The precursor lesion and the carcinoma carry the same trace, non-productive HPV signal, so the group is not averaging two different phenomena.

The transcript program itself makes the distinction visible (@fig-orf). Read gene by gene, the productive groups run the complete viral program, capsid genes included: `r pp(stats$orf_ctrl_l1)`% of productive-control libraries and `r pp(stats$orf_ev_l1)`% of EV biopsies carry L1 reads (@fig-orf a). Skin and neoplasia are not a truncated version of that program but a uniformly faint one, low across the whole genome alike (unselected skin `r pp(stats$orf_skin_e6)`% for E6 and `r pp(stats$orf_skin_l1)`% for L1), which is the signature of a trace rather than of a life cycle arrested before its late phase. Cell lines are the third shape and the one that matters for provenance: E6 and E7 in `r pp(stats$orf_cl_e6)`% and `r pp(stats$orf_cl_e7)`% of libraries against E2 in `r pp(stats$orf_cl_e2)`% and L2 in `r pp(stats$orf_cl_l2)`%, the integrated pattern of @fig-integration generalized from one ratio to the whole genome. Where there are enough reads to apportion, the same contrast appears as composition (@fig-orf b): productive controls place `r pp(stats$orfc_ctrl_late)`% of their viral reads on the late genes against `r pp(stats$orfc_ctrl_onco)`% on E6 and E7, and cell lines invert this exactly, `r pp(stats$orfc_cl_late)`% late against `r pp(stats$orfc_cl_onco)`% oncogenic. Both of those are group-level summaries; read one library at a time, the same separation falls out of the productive criterion itself, with the productive controls and EV biopsies lying above the L1 ≥ 3 threshold and skin and neoplasia below it (@fig-orf c).

::: {#fig-orf}
![](figure3.png)

The viral transcriptional program by sample group. Every panel is conditional on HPV positivity and successful transcript classification, so this figure describes the program of detected infections and is not a prevalence statement; the `r comma(stats$orf_n)` libraries with a classification are distributed unevenly across groups, and each group's *n* is printed on the panel. E5 is omitted, being absent from most beta- and gamma-types and zero in every group here. (**a**) Program breadth: the percentage of a group's libraries carrying at least one read on each open reading frame, as a Beta-Binomial posterior mean under a weakly-informative Beta(0.5, 0.5) prior, as elsewhere in this work. Three shapes separate. Productive controls and EV transcribe the entire genome including the capsid genes; unselected skin and neoplasia are uniformly low across all six frames; cell-line and engineered libraries carry the integrated signature directly, with the oncogenes retained and E2 and the late genes lost. (**b**) Program composition: the mean share of a library's viral reads falling on each frame, stacked in genome order. Restricted to libraries with at least 20 viral reads, because composition is not estimable below that and a single read would otherwise determine a library's entire profile; the surviving *n* is printed per bar, and for unselected skin it is `r stats$orfc_skin_n` of `r comma(stats$uns_n)`, so this panel describes the shape of detectable infections in that group and not the group. (**c**) The productive criterion itself: early-region reads against L1 major-capsid reads for each library, with the L1 ≥ 3 threshold drawn. The vertical axis is L1 rather than the whole late region so that the line is exactly the rule applied throughout, and the productive controls and EV biopsies separate from skin and neoplasia along it.
:::

Tissue that cannot host the virus fixes the meaning of that trace. Papillomaviruses replicate only in differentiating stratified squamous epithelium, so cutaneous adipose, blood and neural material offer no permissive compartment at all; the `r stats$npt_n` such libraries nonetheless carried a trace HPV read at `r pp(stats$npt_pctany)`%, indistinguishable from the `r pp(stats$uns_pctany)`% of unselected skin, while `r pp(stats$npt_pctfloor)`% reached the detection floor and not one yielded a single assignable HPV type. The background rate of trace HPV reads is therefore not a measure of infection: it is the assay's floor, reproduced at the same level in tissue where infection is biologically impossible. Read against that control, the trace signal in unselected skin and in neoplasia is what a library returns when no productive infection is present.

Most of the small floor-level excess is in fact attributable to a handful of libraries the broadened SCC/CIN query captured: `r stats$cin_n` of the `r stats$neo_pos_floor` above-floor neoplasia libraries are high-risk *mucosal* HPV16 cases in squamous-cell carcinoma, conservatively retained in the neoplasia group (@supptbl-cin). Excluding them halves the effect, lowering cutaneous-neoplasia floor-level detection to `r pp(stats$neo_pctfloor_cut)`% (OR vs skin `r fo(stats$m2b_or_cut)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2b_p_cut)`) and strengthening the productivity contrast against warts/EV (OR `r fo(stats$m3_or_cut)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m3_p_cut)`), so the retained group is the conservative choice.

### The assay detects bona fide productive cutaneous HPV, including genuine infections in primary skin

That the trace neoplasia signal reflects biology rather than assay insensitivity is established by the positive controls, which the pipeline detects robustly. Among targeted wart/EV libraries, `r round(stats$m3_ctrl_pct)`% (`r stats$m3_ctrl_prod`/`r stats$m3_ctrl_n`) met the strict productive criterion (≥3 L1 major-capsid reads), spanning the classic cutaneous repertoire: wart-associated alpha types (HPV2, HPV27, HPV57), low-risk mucocutaneous types (HPV6, HPV11), and beta/gamma types (@supptbl-types). Productive infection was significantly more frequent in these controls than among HPV-positive neoplasia libraries (`r round(stats$m3_neo_pct)`%, `r stats$m3_neo_prod`/`r stats$m3_neo_n`; Fisher exact OR `r fo(stats$m3_or)`, 95% CI `r oci(stats$m3_lo, stats$m3_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m3_p)`).

Even so, a minority of genuine, non-cell-line skin lesions did harbor unambiguous productive infection, showing that the trace-level population result does not exclude real cutaneous HPV disease. The strongest cases were a cSCC skin library productively infected with the beta-type HPV12 (99.8% genome coverage; L1 = 1,803, L2 = 3,546 reads), two HPV16-productive cSCC libraries, and two libraries from cutaneous actinic-keratosis/cSCC cohorts whose SRA records carry no tissue field (an actinic keratosis and a carcinoma) co-infected with the beta types HPV96 and HPV182 at near-complete genome coverage (98–99%) and high depth (60–245×), with hundreds of L1 and L2 reads each (@supptbl-productive). These represent the answer to the productive-infection question: bona fide, high-confidence productive beta/gamma-HPV infections do occur in primary skin and skin-associated lesions, but they are the exception against a null background. They do not answer the non-traditional-tissue question, because the residual group that would have to supply that evidence is defined by the *absence* of a site keyword rather than by an identified non-cutaneous site: the two co-infected libraries above sit there only because their cutaneous cohorts record no tissue field at all.

### The HPV type landscape is partitioned by population

The HPV-type-by-group catalog (@supptbl-types, drawn against the detection level in @suppfig-types) recapitulates these conclusions in a single descriptive view, and the corrected grouping sharpens it. The high-risk mucosal types HPV16/HPV18 are confined almost entirely to cell-line material (`r ciA("HPV16","cell_line")` and `r ciA("HPV18","cell_line")` of cell-line libraries). Productive controls are dominated by cutaneous wart types (HPV57, HPV2, HPV27) plus the low-risk mucocutaneous HPV6/HPV11 and gamma types (HPV4, HPV-mKN1). The EV group carries precisely the beta-types the syndrome is defined by (HPV9, HPV14, HPV20, HPV25, HPV47) alongside an alpha co-detection. Unselected skin, by contrast, contributes no HPV type at all above the two-library display threshold except two HPV18 contamination calls: its beta/gamma reservoir is real but sits entirely below the assignment threshold, and is recovered only at the detection level (below). The genuine neoplasia-associated productive infections are the beta/alpha types noted above (HPV12, HPV16, HPV96, HPV182). Collapsed from type to genus (@fig-genus), the same partition is a single picture: productive controls are alpha with a gamma minority, EV biopsies are essentially pure beta (`r kG("Beta","EV")` libraries), cell lines are alpha, and unselected skin is flat and low across alpha, beta and gamma, with the study's only nu detections. Cutaneous neoplasia is the one tissue group in which beta exceeds alpha (`r ciG("Beta","Neoplasia")` versus `r ciG("Alpha","Neoplasia")`), the genus-level shadow of a beta-HPV footprint. The epidemiological reservoir of cutaneous beta/gamma HPV in healthy skin is therefore real but transcriptionally quiet, productive disease is the property of warts and EV, and HPV-associated cutaneous neoplasia carries the virus, when at all, as a trace, non-productive footprint.

Extending this catalog below the assignment threshold answers the descriptive question of *which* types make up the trace. A detection-level re-map of the HPV-positive but untyped libraries, taking the best-hit reference from unique alignments at sub-threshold coverage, resolved a confident low-coverage type for `r stats$trace_resolved` of `r stats$trace_n` such libraries across `r stats$trace_ntypes` types (@supptbl-trace). This recovers the expected commensal signal at the sensitivity floor: healthy skin carried a diverse cutaneous reservoir (`r stats$trace_skin_cut` of `r stats$trace_skin_n` resolved skin calls were beta-, gamma- or nu-types, including HPV12/HPV20, HPV4/HPV65/HPV134 and candidate skin-virome types), cutaneous neoplasia the carcinoma-associated beta and gamma types (HPV5, HPV12, HPV182, HPV222), while the mucosal HPV16/HPV18 signal stayed confined to cell-line material and a low-level contamination overlay. These are low-coverage, non-productive detections that identify the type without bearing on productivity, and so extend the type catalog rather than qualify the trace-not-productive conclusion.

A further descriptive feature of the catalog is that types frequently co-occur: `r cf$libs` of the `r cf$typed` typed libraries carry two or more assigned references, up to five in one library (@supptbl-coinf). Because coverage is scored from uniquely-mapped reads alone, cross-mapping between similar types cannot generate these calls. The commonest pairing is HPV11 with HPV42, which co-occur in `r cf$both1142` libraries, against `r cf$only42` carrying HPV42 alone. We present this as a hypothesis rather than a finding, for the three reasons set out in @supptbl-coinf. The co-infected libraries are heavily pseudo-replicated, `r cf$pair_libs` of the `r cf$libs` coming from `r cf$pair_donors` donors of one study, each sequenced in three fractions across two SRA submissions; the secondary type in a co-infection is usually near the detection threshold (median depth `r p1(cf$sec_med_depth)`×, `r cf$sec_shallow`% below 5×), to the point that one donor's MeRIP input and IP fractions call different second types; and requiring both partners to clear a stricter coverage bar leaves `r cf$strict_libs` HPV11/HPV42 libraries from `r cf$strict_donors` of those `r cf$pair_donors` donors. Whether the pairing reflects genuine dual infection, or only that a second type is called where it happens to be abundant, cannot be settled from this material. The pattern is worth testing in a cohort assembled for the purpose; it cannot be resolved here.


::: {#fig-genus}
![](figure4.png)

HPV genus prevalence by sample group. The two type catalogs are collapsed from HPV type to HPV genus: the assigned-type catalog of @supptbl-types (top row), the detection-level trace catalog of @supptbl-trace (middle row), and their union (bottom row), a library contributing to at most one of the first two rows. Each point is the prevalence of that genus within that sample group, meaning the percentage of the group's libraries in which the genus was detected, estimated as a Beta-Binomial posterior mean under a weakly-informative Beta(0.5, 0.5) prior; the vertical bar through it is the 95% credible interval of that estimate, so it shows how firmly the prevalence is pinned and is wide wherever a group is small. The estimator is the one used in the two tables, so a point here and the corresponding table cell quote the same number. The figure printed above each point is the count of libraries in which the genus was detected; the denominator is the group size (Methods). Gray crosses mark groups in which a genus was never detected; they sit at the axis floor because the *y*-axis is log-scaled and the lowest tick, labeled 0, is a placeholder for zero. A library carrying two types of different genera contributes to both, so the points within a group need not sum to that group's positivity rate. Read across the bottom row, the figure is the type landscape of the study in one panel: the productive controls are alpha-dominated (`r kG("Alpha","Productive controls")` libraries, `r ciG("Alpha","Productive controls")`) with a gamma minority (`r ciG("Gamma","Productive controls")`) and no beta at all, the repertoire of cutaneous and mucocutaneous warts; the EV biopsies are the mirror image, essentially pure beta (`r kG("Beta","EV")`, `r ciG("Beta","EV")`), the genus the syndrome is defined by; cell lines are alpha (`r ciG("Alpha","Cell line")`), the integrated HPV16/HPV18 contamination signature; unselected skin is flat and low, with alpha, beta and gamma at indistinguishable rates near `r ciG("Beta","Unselected skin")` and the study's only nu detections (`r kG("Nu","Unselected skin")` libraries, HPV41), the profile of a sparse commensal reservoir rather than of any one disease; and cutaneous neoplasia is the one tissue group in which beta exceeds alpha (`r ciG("Beta","Neoplasia")` versus `r ciG("Alpha","Neoplasia")`), consistent with a beta-HPV footprint, though at prevalences one to two orders of magnitude below the productive groups. The mu genus (HPV1, the classic plantar-wart type) was detected in no group.

### The reservoir the survey is silent against is visible in independent public DNA

A transcriptional survey can only report silence against a reservoir whose existence it assumes, and every group above is an RNA measurement made in one pipeline. To test the assumption outside RNA and outside this cohort, we re-tabulated the petabase-scale papillomavirus catalog of public metagenome assemblies [@shenpv2026; @chikhi2024] by body site (Methods). Skin metagenomes contribute `r comma(rvn("n_skin_lib"))` HPV-positive libraries whose genus composition is the cutaneous commensal profile: beta in `r p1(rvn("skin_beta"))`% and gamma in `r p1(rvn("skin_gamma"))`% of those libraries, against alpha in `r p1(rvn("skin_alpha"))`% and mu in `r p1(rvn("skin_mu"))`% (@fig-reservoir). These are compositions conditional on positivity, with the HPV-positive libraries of a body site as the denominator; no prevalence is quoted from this catalog, and none is needed for the comparison made here. That the read-out carries signal rather than assembly noise is established by applying the identical procedure to the other body sites (@suppfig-reservoir-gut), which recovers the textbook mucosal niche from vaginal DNA alone (alpha `r p1(rvn("vaginal_alpha"))`%, beta `r p1(rvn("vaginal_beta"))`%, gamma `r p1(rvn("vaginal_gamma"))`%), with its classic high- and low-risk repertoire (HPV91, HPV51, HPV66, HPV67, HPV16, HPV90). Gut metagenomes in the same figure interleave mucosal alpha with cutaneous beta, the signature of a collection route that crosses perianal skin, and are therefore a control on the sampling route rather than a third reservoir.

The types are where the two modalities meet, and they do not agree. The `r rv("top_n")` commonest skin types in the DNA reservoir are `r rv("topn_types")`, led by `r rv("top_type")` in `r p1(rvn("top_type_pct"))`% of HPV-positive skin libraries: beta and gamma types throughout except HPV2, the repertoire that our detection level recovers only as a trace (@supptbl-trace) and that the assigned catalog of @supptbl-types does not record in a single unselected-skin library. Set against our own `r comma(rvn("n_skin_rna"))` unselected-skin libraries, those `r rv("top_n")` types together account for `r rvn("topn_rna_assigned")` assigned detections and `r rvn("topn_rna_trace")` trace-level detections (@fig-reservoir a). Read across every type rather than the commonest few, the disagreement is the general case and not a property of the commonest few: `r rv("n_dna_present_silent")` of the `r rv("n_dna_present")` types present in the skin DNA reservoir are productive in no library of this study, `r rv("n_prod_dna_absent")` of the `r rv("n_prod_types")` productive types are absent from skin DNA altogether, and `r rv("corner_types")` alone is both abundant in the reservoir and productive here (@fig-reservoir b). HPV8, the beta type most consistently associated with cutaneous carcinoma in the serological and DNA literature, is the sharpest case: `r rv("hpv8_dna")` of the `r comma(rvn("n_skin_lib"))` HPV-positive skin DNA libraries carry it, against `r rv("hpv8_rna_all")` of the `r comma(rvn("n_rna_all"))` RNA libraries screened here at any level, assigned or trace. The reservoir this survey finds transcriptionally quiet is therefore not an assumption of the survey: it is independently present, in the expected genera and the expected types, in a different molecule and a different set of studies.

Two further features of the DNA composition bear on the reference-panel limit of any typing scheme, ours included. `r p1(rvn("skin_unresolved"))`% of HPV-positive skin libraries carry a contig that cannot be placed in a genus and `r p1(rvn("skin_novel_any"))`% carry a cluster with no reference match at all, against `r p1(rvn("vaginal_unresolved"))`% and `r p1(rvn("vaginal_novel_any"))`% respectively in the vaginal libraries. The mucosal alpha types are exhaustively described and the cutaneous reservoir is not, consistent with the 229 skin types described without a reference genome [@bzhalava2014], so both the DNA composition above and our own type catalog are lower bounds on cutaneous diversity. The two arms also sample different compartments, surface swabs against bulk tissue, which we return to in the Discussion.

### A Bayesian re-analysis under weakly-informative priors confirms the contrasts

To confirm these conclusions are not artifacts of the frequentist framework or of the near-complete separation in the strongest contrast, we refitted the positivity, depth-controlled detection and productivity models as Bayesian logistic regressions under weakly-informative priors (Normal(0, 2.5) on the log-odds coefficients; Methods), summarizing each effect by its posterior median odds ratio, 95% credible interval (CrI) and posterior probability of direction (@supptbl-bayes, drawn as a forest plot in @suppfig-bayes). The contamination enrichment and the trace excess were reproduced essentially unchanged and with near-certainty (cell-line OR `r bor(bget("M1_cell_line"))`, engineered OR `r bor(bget("M1_engineered"))`, neoplasia trace OR `r bor(bget("M2a_neoplasia_vs_skin_any"))`; each with P(OR > 1) > 0.999). Crucially, the productive-controls-versus-skin contrast, whose frequentist odds ratio (`r fo(stats$fish_or)`) is inflated and unstable under separation, regularized to a finite but still enormous posterior OR of `r bor(bget("M2c_controls_vs_skin_floor"))` (`r bor(bget("M2c_controls_vs_skin_floor_studentt"))` under a heavier-tailed Student-*t* prior): the productive gap between warts/EV and skin is real, not a separation artifact. Deeper sequencing within neoplasia again bought no productive-level detection (OR `r bor(bget("M2d_depth_within_neoplasia"))`, P(OR > 1) = `r pdir(bget("M2d_depth_within_neoplasia")$p_gt1)`), and the warts/EV-versus-neoplasia productivity contrast held (OR `r bor(bget("M3_controls_vs_neoplasia"))`, P(OR > 1) = `r pdir(bget("M3_controls_vs_neoplasia")$p_gt1)`). The neoplasia-versus-skin comparison at floor level, whose frequentist interval is wide because it rests on `r stats$neo_pos_floor` above-floor libraries, shrinks under the prior but stays clearly positive (OR `r bor(bget("M2b_neoplasia_vs_skin_floor"))`, P(OR > 1) = `r pdir(bget("M2b_neoplasia_vs_skin_floor")$p_gt1)`): the small floor-level elevation of neoplasia over clean skin is genuine. It is nonetheless negligible beside the near-four-orders-of-magnitude productive-control effect, and it does not alter the trace-not-productive conclusion.
